summary: This work demonstrates that operating cryogenic quantum amplifiers in the nonlinear regime, rather than optimizing for linear quantum-limited performance, can enhance single-shot quantum state classification when the measurement chain is end-to-end optimized for task-specific objectives. The analysis uses two coupled SNAIL oscillators—a squeezer for state preparation and a nonlinear analyzer—and shows that exploiting Kerr nonlinearity to transduce information encoded in higher-order moments achieves classification fidelities approaching unity in regimes where linear amplification fails.
motivation: Conventional cryogenic readout chains optimize amplifier performance by maximizing signal-to-noise ratio in the linear regime, an objective well-suited for parameter estimation but suboptimal for quantum state discrimination tasks. This work investigates whether deliberate nonlinear amplifier operation can provide practical advantages for measurement tasks beyond parameter estimation, grounded in superconducting qubit readout architectures.
method: A two-SNAIL system with unidirectional coupling was modeled via a stochastic quantum master equation with third- and fourth-order nonlinearities. State discrimination between squeezed vacuum states with orthogonal squeezing directions was analyzed using truncated cumulant equations of motion, performance metrics (mean separation and Fisher discriminant), and end-to-end optimization over externally tunable pump and signal drive strengths and phases, with numerical solutions validated against analytical perturbative expressions in the weak-nonlinearity limit.
result: Optimal nonlinear operation achieved classification fidelity of 1.0 (versus 0.84 for linear operation) for zero-mean pointer states distinguished only by second moments. The optimal dispersive shift for qubit readout without cavity displacement was found to be $\chi \approx 0.2\kappa$, substantially lower than the conventional $\chi_\mathrm{opt,disp} = \kappa/2$, and performance degraded gracefully with downstream classical noise $n_\mathrm{cl}$ from room-temperature electronics.
